cases.abstract: Personalizing text-to-image generation requires retaining a particular subject's identity while producing images beyond the few available views. We introduce DreamBooth, which fine-tunes a pretrained diffusion model on three to five subject images, associating a rare-token identifier with the subject's class. This association draws on the class prior to support new contexts, poses, and appearances. A class-specific prior-preservation loss uses images generated by the original model to limit class collapse and preserve output diversity during personalization. We also provide a public evaluation suite covering 30 subjects and 25 prompts per subject, together with a DINO-based subject-fidelity metric. On Stable Diffusion, DreamBooth achieves DINO similarity of 0.668 versus 0.569 and text-image CLIP similarity of 0.305 versus 0.255 for Textual Inversion. Human preference rates are 68% for subject fidelity and 81% for prompt fidelity. Imagen ablations show that prior preservation reduces class collapse and increases diversity, but slightly lowers subject fidelity. Qualitative results include recontextualization, artistic renditions, novel views, and property changes; context-appearance entanglement, overfitting, and hallucinated subject details remain failure modes.
cases.notes: Central contribution: few-shot identity-preserving personalization, not generic image adaptation. Same-backbone Stable Diffusion comparisons and human preferences provide decisive evidence; Imagen ablations establish the diversity/identity tradeoff. Retained the public evaluation resource and identity-sensitive metric as co-contributions. Class priors are the design rationale; ablations support their tested role rather than universal causality. Failures qualify novel-image generation. Preference percentages are majority-vote outcomes, not task-success rates.

cases.abstract: Toolformer learns when and how to call external tools using a language model's own prediction loss rather than task-specific tool-use supervision. Given a few demonstrations per tool, the model proposes calls in ordinary text; executed calls are retained when their responses improve subsequent token prediction over both no-call and call-only alternatives. Fine-tuning on this augmented text teaches tool selection, argument generation, and response incorporation. With GPT-J and five text-based APIs, prompted zero-shot evaluation allows at most one call per input. On ASDiv, answer accuracy reaches 40.4%, compared with 9.6% for GPT-J fine-tuned on the corresponding text without calls and 14.0% for GPT-3 (175B). Toolformer also improves factual completion and temporal benchmarks; question answering exceeds GPT-J baselines but remains below GPT-3. Translation calls help across evaluated languages without consistently surpassing unmodified GPT-J. With calls disabled, language-modeling perplexity matches the text-only fine-tuning baseline on both evaluated corpora. A GPT-2 size sweep places useful tool use near 775M parameters, with search an exception; stronger base models can diminish weaker tools' utility. Independent call generation leaves chained and interactive tool use unsupported, bounding the demonstrated gains to noninteractive tool access.
cases.notes: Central contribution: self-supervised acquisition of tool-use decisions, established by loss-filtered augmentation and gains over text-only and tool-disabled GPT-J controls. ASDiv provides a decisive comparison; mixed QA and multilingual outcomes prevent a general-superiority claim. Perplexity parity is only against text-only fine-tuning with calls disabled, not against original pretraining or active-tool generation. Retained scaling findings and the one-call/chaining boundary. Reported task scores use the source's permissive answer criteria; no exact-match or autonomous multi-step claim is implied.
